title: What are the 7 Rs of cloud migration (Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Refactor), and how do you choose per application?
shortTitle: What are the 7 Rs of cloud migration, and how do you choose per application?
topicTitle: What are the 7 Rs of cloud migration

s1_definition.profdef: The 7 Rs are the seven migration strategies for moving an application portfolio to the cloud — Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, and Refactor — each representing a different balance of migration effort against long-term cloud benefit. You choose per application by assessing its business value, technical fit, cost, and risk, so that low-value systems are decommissioned, poorly-fitting ones stay put, and high-value ones get the investment to become cloud-native. The decision is made application by application, never one blanket strategy for the whole estate.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India is moving its old head office into a brand-new building. Some filing cabinets are full of expired forms, so you just throw them away (Retire). Some legacy machines are too fragile to move, so you leave them in the old office for now (Retain). Some desks you simply pick up and put in the new building unchanged (Rehost). Some you move as a whole department pod without rearranging (Relocate). Some old equipment you replace by subscribing to a modern service instead (Repurchase). Some you tweak a little to fit the new building's wiring (Replatform). And the most important systems you completely redesign to take full advantage of the new building (Refactor). You decide item by item, because treating everything the same wastes money and effort.
s1_definition.oneliner: Seven strategies from "throw it away" to "rebuild it cloud-native," chosen one application at a time by weighing effort against value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 7 Rs are the seven migration strategies for moving an application portfolio to the cloud — Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, and Refactor — each representing a different balance of migration effort against long-term cloud benefit. You choose per application by assessing its business value, technical fit, cost, and risk, so that low-value systems are decommissioned, poorly-fitting ones stay put, and high-value ones get the investment to become cloud-native. The decision is made application by application, never one blanket strategy for the whole estate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India is moving its old head office into a brand-new building. Some filing cabinets are full of expired forms, so you just throw them away (Retire). Some legacy machines are too fragile to move, so you leave them in the old office for now (Retain). Some desks you simply pick up and put in the new building unchanged (Rehost). Some you move as a whole department pod without rearranging (Relocate). Some old equipment you replace by subscribing to a modern service instead (Repurchase). Some you tweak a little to fit the new building's wiring (Replatform). And the most important systems you completely redesign to take full advantage of the new building (Refactor). You decide item by item, because treating everything the same wastes money and effort.

**One line to remember:** Seven strategies from "throw it away" to "rebuild it cloud-native," chosen one application at a time by weighing effort against value.

sections.s2_technical:
Each R is a distinct answer to the question "what should we do with this application?" Retire means you decommission it entirely — portfolio assessments routinely find that a meaningful slice of applications are redundant or unused, and the cheapest migration is the one you do not do. Retain, sometimes called revisit, means you deliberately keep the application where it is for now, usually because it has a hard dependency, a looming retirement date, a compliance constraint, or simply because the business case to move it is not there yet. Both of these are about reducing the scope of the migration before you spend a rupee moving anything.

Rehost, often called lift-and-shift, means moving the application to cloud infrastructure with no code changes — the same virtual machines, just running in the cloud. It is fast and low-risk, which makes it attractive for large estates under time pressure, but it captures only basic benefits like data-center exit and does not take advantage of managed services. Relocate is a special fast path where you move an entire environment, such as a VMware estate, to the cloud without changing the hypervisor, operating systems, or application — it is lift-and-shift at the platform level with minimal disruption.

Repurchase, sometimes called drop-and-shop, means replacing the application with a different product, typically moving from a self-managed or licensed system to a software-as-a-service subscription — for example retiring a self-hosted email or CRM in favor of a managed offering. You stop operating the software yourself and consume it as a service. Replatform, often called lift-tinker-and-shift, means making a few targeted cloud optimizations without changing the core architecture — the classic example is moving a self-managed database onto a managed database service so you keep the application mostly intact but hand off patching, backups, and high availability to the platform.

Refactor, also called re-architect, is the deepest and most expensive strategy: you significantly change the application to become cloud-native, perhaps breaking a monolith into microservices, adopting serverless, or redesigning around managed queues and event streams. It costs the most and carries the most risk, but it delivers the most benefit — elasticity, resilience, and long-term agility — so you reserve it for the applications where that payoff clearly justifies the investment.

Choosing per application is a structured assessment, and this is the senior-level discipline. You inventory the whole estate and score each application on business value, technical complexity, cloud suitability, cost to migrate, and risk. Low-value or unused applications go to Retire. Applications with blocking dependencies or near end-of-life go to Retain. High-volume, low-complexity applications under time pressure go to Rehost or Relocate to exit the data center quickly. Applications backed by a better commercial product go to Repurchase. Applications that would benefit from a managed database or runtime with little code change go to Replatform. And the strategic, high-value applications that the business depends on for differentiation go to Refactor, because only there does the deep investment pay off. The mistake to avoid is applying one R to everything — a pure lift-and-shift of the whole estate leaves you paying cloud prices for data-center-shaped workloads, while trying to refactor everything blows the budget and timeline.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the migration office is assessing four applications and must assign each the right R, then estimate the relative effort so leadership can sequence the program sensibly.

Problem 1 — An old internal expense-reporting tool has not been logged into for two years and a newer system already does the job. This is exactly where Retire fits — the cheapest migration is deleting a redundant application, and keeping it would waste money moving dead weight.

Problem 2 — A mainframe-linked settlement adapter has a hard dependency on hardware that cannot move yet and is scheduled for replacement next year. This is exactly where Retain fits — forcing it to the cloud now would be high-risk for a system about to be retired anyway.

Problem 3 — A self-managed PostgreSQL behind the customer-accounts service is stable, but the team spends too much time on patching and backups. This is exactly where Replatform fits — moving it to a managed database keeps the application nearly unchanged while the platform takes over the operational burden.

Problem 4 — The core payments monolith is the bank's most strategic system, but it cannot scale for peak festival-season traffic and releases are slow. This is exactly where Refactor fits — the high business value justifies the expensive re-architecture into scalable services.

The code will model a `MigrationStrategy` with a relative effort score, an `Application` carrying an assessment, a `MigrationAdvisor` that recommends the right R from the assessment signals, and a `PortfolioPlanner` that totals the effort and orders the applications. We will run the four applications and print each recommendation plus the overall plan.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# portfolio.yml — assessment inputs per application
applications:
  expense-tool:
    used: false
    businessValue: low
  settlement-adapter:
    blockingDependency: true
    nearEndOfLife: true
  customer-accounts-db:
    operationalBurdenHigh: true
    codeChangeTolerance: low
  payments-monolith:
    businessValue: high
    needsElasticity: true
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four applications — an unused expense tool, a settlement adapter with a blocking dependency and near end-of-life, a customer-accounts database with high operational burden, and the strategic payments monolith that needs elasticity.

Step 1: The planner takes the portfolio and starts a running effort total at zero, then asks the advisor to recommend an R for each application in order.

Step 2: The advisor evaluates the expense tool. Its very first check is whether the application is used; it is not, so the advisor immediately returns Retire. Retire has an effort of zero. The planner records expense-tool as Retire and the total effort stays at zero.

Step 3: The advisor evaluates the settlement adapter. It is used, so the first check fails, but the next check — a blocking dependency or near end-of-life — is true, so the advisor returns Retain. Retain also has an effort of zero. The planner records it and the total stays at zero.

Step 4: The advisor evaluates the customer-accounts database. It is used, has no blocking dependency, and is not high-value-plus-elastic, but its operational burden is high, so the advisor returns Replatform. Replatform has an effort of five. The planner records it and the total becomes five.

Step 5: The advisor evaluates the payments monolith. It is used, has no blocking dependency, and is both high business value and in need of elasticity, so the advisor returns Refactor. Refactor has an effort of nine. The planner records it and the total becomes fourteen.

Step 6: The planner finishes with four recommendations and a total relative effort of fourteen. Notice that the two zero-effort decisions, Retire and Retain, shrank the real migration scope before any work was spent, while the effort is concentrated on the two applications where cloud benefit actually justifies it. This is precisely the per-application discipline the 7 Rs are meant to enforce.

Final output:

```
INFO: === National Bank of India — cloud migration assessment ===
INFO: [expense-tool] → RETIRE (effort 0)
INFO: [settlement-adapter] → RETAIN (effort 0)
INFO: [customer-accounts-db] → REPLATFORM (effort 5)
INFO: [payments-monolith] → REFACTOR (effort 9)
INFO: Portfolio plan complete — total relative effort = 14
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 7 Rs are the seven strategies for moving an application portfolio to the cloud, and the whole point is that you choose one per application rather than applying a single blanket approach to the entire estate. Retire means you decommission an application entirely, because portfolio assessments always find redundant or unused systems and the cheapest migration is the one you never do. Retain means you deliberately leave an application where it is for now, usually because of a hard dependency, a looming retirement date, or a compliance constraint. Both of these shrink the scope before you spend anything on moving.

Rehost is lift-and-shift — you move the application to cloud infrastructure with no code change, which is fast and low-risk but only captures basic benefits like exiting the data center. Relocate is a fast path for moving an entire platform such as a VMware estate without changing the hypervisor or operating systems. Repurchase is drop-and-shop — you replace the application with a different product, typically moving from self-managed software to a software-as-a-service subscription so you stop operating it yourself. Replatform is lift-tinker-and-shift — you make a few targeted optimizations without changing the core architecture, the classic example being moving a self-managed database onto a managed database service so the platform takes over patching and backups. And Refactor is the deepest and most expensive — you re-architect the application to be cloud-native, perhaps breaking a monolith into services or going serverless, which costs and risks the most but delivers the most long-term agility.

The way I choose is a structured assessment. I inventory the estate and score each application on business value, technical complexity, cloud suitability, migration cost, and risk. Unused systems go to Retire, blocked or end-of-life ones go to Retain, high-volume low-complexity ones under time pressure go to Rehost or Relocate, ones with a better commercial product go to Repurchase, ones that just need their operational burden lifted go to Replatform, and the strategic high-value systems the business depends on go to Refactor, because only there does the deep investment pay off. The mistake I actively avoid is one R for everything — a pure lift-and-shift of the whole estate leaves you paying cloud prices for data-center-shaped workloads, while refactoring everything blows the budget.

At National Bank of India I ran exactly this assessment and even built a small advisor to make it repeatable. It retired an expense tool nobody had used in two years, retained a mainframe settlement adapter that was due for replacement anyway, replatformed our customer-accounts database onto a managed service to stop the team drowning in patching, and refactored the strategic payments monolith into scalable services because it genuinely needed to handle festival-season peaks. The two zero-effort decisions shrank the migration scope up front, and the real investment landed only where the cloud benefit clearly justified it — which is the whole discipline the 7 Rs are designed to enforce.
